episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. transcript_window.text: What I do think they have in terms of peakness is peak integration.
I don't think anybody has done it as well as they have.
And it's not just their lighting products.

Their lighting products, their sensors, and by the way, they make amongst the best sensors on the market, and their buttons and remotes, it's all accessible through all these other ecosystems, which is smart, smart, smart.
And I remember, especially in those early days when Alexa, Google Assistant, and then HomeKit were all really on the come up.
They were all so different that I feel like I spent a lot of my time, and I'm sure you both spent a lot of your time, just explaining to people what worked with what.
And having Hue just be a yes was such an unbelievable victory that it was like, I actually don't have to ask about all the other things in your house.
